said: In December two thousand one, Enron, a company that reported sixty-three billion dollars in assets, collapsed in what was then the biggest bankruptcy in American history.
For six years in a row, Fortune magazine named it America's most innovative company. Business schools taught its success story. Wall Street loved it.
Enron was formed in nineteen eighty-five, when two natural gas pipeline companies merged. Its boss was Ken Lay, a friendly economist with a doctorate.
Then he hired a sharp young consultant named Jeff Skilling. Skilling had a big idea. Enron shouldn't just move gas. It should trade it, like a stock.
The rule was called mark-to-market accounting. In nineteen ninety-two, regulators allowed Enron to use it for its contracts.
Imagine a lemonade stand that signs a deal to sell lemonade every summer for twenty years. It tells everyone it already made twenty years of profit, today.
One famous example was a deal with the video store chain Blockbuster to stream movies over the internet. It barely worked. Enron still booked over a hundred million dollars of expected profit.
Enron's chief financial officer was Andrew Fastow. His job was to make the company's money look good. He became very creative at it.
Fastow also gave himself a special deal. He personally ran some of these side companies, and earned more than thirty million dollars from them.
Enron's outside auditor, the famous firm Arthur Andersen, signed off on the books year after year. Andersen was also earning huge consulting fees from Enron.
In March two thousand one, a young Fortune reporter named Bethany McLean published an article with a simple title. Is Enron overpriced?

what: highlight "The Smartest Guys in the Room"
said: Skilling reportedly called her questions unethical. A few weeks later, on a call with investors, he insulted an analyst who asked why Enron wouldn't share its full financial statements.
That spring, there was another warning. California had suffered an electricity crisis, with blackouts and soaring prices. Later evidence showed Enron traders had helped make it worse.
A few days later, an Enron executive named Sherron Watkins wrote a letter to Ken Lay. She warned that the company might implode in a wave of accounting scandals.
A week later, the S E C opened an investigation. Then Enron admitted it had overstated its profits for years, by hundreds of millions of dollars.
Banks stopped lending to Enron. Its trading partners demanded cash up front. A rival company, Dynegy, agreed to buy Enron, then backed out after looking at the books.
By late November, the stock was worth less than one dollar. On December second, two thousand one, Enron filed for bankruptcy.

said: That conviction was later overturned on appeal. But by then, the firm was already gone.
In two thousand six, a jury convicted Jeff Skilling and Ken Lay. Skilling was sentenced to twenty-four years, later reduced. Lay died of a heart attack before he could be sentenced.
Congress also acted fast. In two thousand two, it passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Now, top executives must personally sign off that their company's financial reports are true.
If they knowingly sign false numbers, they can go to prison. Auditors are now watched by a new oversight board, and there are stricter limits on selling them extra consulting work.
